content_map.problem: A request or job may be handled by a different process after scaling, restart, deploy or relocation, so correctness cannot depend on data surviving inside one process's memory or local filesystem.
content_map.thesis: Run application processes as stateless, share-nothing execution units; keep any data that must survive requests/jobs in stateful backing services, using process-local memory/files only as disposable short-lived cache within the current transaction/work unit.
mechanisms: Do not assume future requests or jobs land on the same process.
Persist durable data in a backing service such as a database rather than process memory or local disk.
Allow memory/filesystem only as brief cache whose loss does not break correctness.
Treat process restart, deploy and relocation as normal events that can erase local state.
Move user session state to a datastore instead of relying on sticky routing to one process.
examples: A process downloads a large file, transforms it and persists the result; the downloaded local file can disappear afterward without correctness loss.
A user's session survives because it is stored externally rather than only in the memory of the process that handled the previous request.
A horizontally scaled worker can be replaced because the next job does not require hidden local memory from the previous instance.
claims: Twelve-factor application processes are stateless and share-nothing.
Data that must persist belongs in a stateful backing service rather than process-local memory or filesystem.
Process-local memory/files can be used only as brief disposable cache because future work may run in a different process and restarts erase local state.
Sticky sessions that depend on one process retaining session state violate the process factor.
evidence: The complete Processes page explicitly states stateless/share-nothing execution and external backing services for persistent data.
The page states that local memory/filesystem can be brief single-transaction cache but must not be assumed available on a future request/job.
The page names restart/deploy/relocation as reasons local process state disappears and rejects sticky-session reliance.
assumptions: A backing service can provide the durability/availability required by the application state it owns.
The execution platform may freely replace or reschedule processes.
Any process-local cache can be recomputed or discarded without violating correctness.
limitations: Stateless processes do not mean the application as a whole has no state; durable state is deliberately moved to backing services.
The factor does not specify how a long-running workflow persists orchestration progress; modern durable runtimes can keep state externally while still using disposable worker processes.
Externalizing state introduces network, consistency, latency and backing-service failure concerns that this short factor does not solve.
The guidance is about runtime process disposability, not a claim that every algorithm or operation must complete in one request or cannot use temporary local working data.
open_questions: Which state belongs in a database, queue, object store or durable workflow service for a specific application?
Where does externalizing every intermediate value create unnecessary latency versus useful disposability?
How should modern long-running workflows separate disposable compute from durable orchestration state?

selection.requested_focus: Understand the stateless/share-nothing process model, why durable state belongs in backing services, and where this principle helps or becomes too simplistic for modern long-running workflows.
coherent_core: A process is disposable and cannot be trusted to serve the next request/job.
Durable correctness state therefore lives outside the process in backing services.
Local memory/files remain useful only when they are disposable/recomputable within the current work unit.
The principle is compatible with modern durable workflows when orchestration state is externalized, but the source itself does not define a workflow engine.
drop_notes: Do not equate generic Twelve-Factor processes with Temporal Worker Processes, Workflow Executions or Activities; the retrieved names are implementation-specific concepts outside this source.
Do not turn 'stateless process' into 'stateless application'; the source explicitly depends on stateful backing services.
connections: durable execution is compatible at a boundary level when workflow state lives outside disposable workers, but it is not the mechanism taught by this source
the same disposability principle applies to horizontally scaled web processes and background workers when durable state is external
